title: Only the practice helps
hookLine: incense fills a memorial hall and follows the version; Atisha's third root names what travels further
tomorrow: you can't take it with you. so what do you do with it now?

cards: At the very end, what actually helps? At a temple memorial, the first thing that reaches you isn't a sight. It's incense, drifting in thin lines, following whatever version the room has.
People bring flowers, fruit, photos, the person's favorite tea. All of it is love. Atisha's third root asks a harder question, about the person who is dying.

teach.h: THE THIRD ROOT: ONLY THE DHARMA.
teach.b: Atisha's three roots began with death is certain, then its time uncertain. The third: at death, only the dharma helps. Only the practice.

teach.h: WEALTH, FRIENDS, EVEN THE BODY STAY.
teach.b: Teachers unfold it in three steps, and the next days take them one by one: wealth doesn't come along; friends and family can't come along; even the body stays.
What's left is the mind and the habits it built: the patience practiced, the kindness repeated, the calm returned to over and over. Now the smell. The Dhammapada has a verse about scent.

teach.h: SCENT THAT GOES AGAINST THE WIND.
teach.b: The fragrance of flowers, it says, doesn't travel against the wind, not sandalwood, not jasmine. But the fragrance of good people travels against the wind; a good person's goodness spreads in every direction.
Incense is lovely, and it only goes where the air carries it. Goodness doesn't wait for a favorable breeze. That's why the third root isn't grim.
It says one thing helps, and it's the one thing that was never in a drawer or a bank: what a person has practiced, and what they've become by practicing.
At the end, when every wind is against you, that's the scent that still travels.

how: At Buddhist memorials, families often offer incense, flowers and food before the person's photo while monks or lay leaders chant; in Vietnamese Pure Land practice, some families chant the name of Amitabha Buddha with a dying relative.

games.q: what does “only the practice helps” mean?
o: at death, only what you've practiced goes with you
a rule that only monks can be helped when dying
the belief that doctors can't help a dying person

games.q: the third root, and the scent — tap the pairs.
p: at death, only the dharma helps
scent goes only with the wind
what a person practiced and became

s: the third root says nothing helps at death
it says one thing helps: what a person has practiced and become.
the Dhammapada says the fragrance of good people travels against the wind
flowers and sandalwood can't; goodness spreads in every direction.
offerings at a memorial are pointless, according to the third root
the offerings are love from the living. the root is about what goes with the one who dies.

games.q: your aunt has a month to live and wants to spend it updating her will and sorting jewelry. she asks you to help. what does the third root suggest?
o: only the will and the jewelry matter now; get them perfect.
help with the papers, and leave room for what goes with her: calm, kindness, practice.
refuse to help with anything practical; it's all worthless now.
games.why: wealth stays behind, but the root doesn't scorn practical love. what goes on with her is what she has practiced: so make room for it.

practice: If there's something with a scent near you, tea, soap, a sleeve, smell it once, slowly, and notice it only reaches you because the air brings it.
Then bring to mind one kind thing someone did for you long ago that still reaches you today. Rest with that second scent, the one that travels against the wind.

wordCard.voice: Only the practice helps: Atisha's third root. At death, what goes on is what a person has practiced and become.

orig.note: Pali: dhamma (Sanskrit dharma), the Buddha's teaching and the practice of it; what the third root says helps.

carryVoice: Your line: only the practice, the scent that travels against the wind. That's day sixteen thirty-five, breathed in.

sources.ref: Atisha's third root (at death, only the dharma helps), as taught in the Tibetan lamrim
Dhammapada 54 (the scent of flowers, sandalwood, tagara and jasmine does not travel against the wind; the scent of good people does)
